company_brief.summary: PostHog is a product and developer-focused platform founded by James Hawkins and Tim Glaser (hatched in Y Combinator’s W20 batch, launched in 2020). Used by 500,000+ teams and run by a company of 230+ people, PostHog aims to make products “self‑driving” and to equip developers to build successful products. The company emphasizes an engineer-first approach, generous free tiers, open source products, honest communication, and long-term independence from private‑equity‑style tactics.
company_brief.what_they_do: PostHog provides a single platform to ingest, store and query product and company data and to stitch analytics, session replays, errors and logs together. Its product suite includes product analytics, session replay, error tracking, web analytics, feature flags, experiments, surveys, managed warehouse, CDP, workflows, logs, AI observability, heatmaps, replay vision, no‑code A/B testing and more. It can pipe in third‑party data from 700+ sources, offers agents and tools (e.g., PostHog MCP and PostHog Desktop) to give product context to engineers, and surfaces findings and actionable recommendations to help ship code and improve products.

role.title: Software Engineer I
responsibilities: Develop and maintain frontend applications using React
Build and maintain backend services using Node.js and related JavaScript technologies

questions.prompt: Build or describe a React component (with Node.js backend) that displays a paginated list of product events for an analytics dashboard. Explain component structure, state management, data fetching, error handling and pagination. Describe how you would add real‑time updates so new events appear without a full refresh.
questions.answer_outline:
- React: functional component using hooks (useState, useEffect, useRef); separate presentational and container components; useContext or Redux only if global state needed
- Data fetching: use fetch/axios in useEffect; include abort controller to cancel stale requests
- State: keep events array, loading, error, pagination cursor/page, hasMore flag
- Pagination: cursor-based API or page/limit; append or replace events depending on UX; support load more and infinite scroll with intersection observer
- Error/loading UX: spinners, toasts, retry button, optimistic UI for client-side actions
- Real-time updates: use WebSockets or Server-Sent Events to push new events; on message, prepend/append to events with deduplication (use event id)
- Backend (Node.js): REST endpoint with cursor/pagination; SSE/WebSocket endpoint broadcasting new events; handle authentication and rate limits
- Performance: batch updates, debounce UI updates, virtualization for long lists (react-window/react-virtualized)
- Security/ops: validate inputs on server, paginate to avoid huge payloads, monitor and backpressure for high event volume

questions.prompt: You maintain a React frontend and Node.js API for PostHog-like analytics. Users report slow initial load and sluggish UI when many components render; the Node API also shows high latency under load. How would you diagnose and fix frontend bundle and runtime performance issues and the Node backend latency? Give concrete techniques and code-level optimizations you would apply.
questions.answer_outline:
Frontend diagnostics:
- Measure: Lighthouse, WebPageTest, Chrome DevTools Performance, React Profiler to find slow renders and large bundles
- Bundle size: analyze with source-map-explorer/webpack-bundle-analyzer; remove unused deps, replace heavy libs, enable tree-shaking
- Code-splitting/lazy loading: dynamic import() to split routes/components; React.lazy + Suspense
- Reduce runtime work: memoize components (React.memo, useMemo, useCallback), avoid unnecessary re-renders by proper keying and prop changes
- Virtualize long lists (react-window) and avoid rendering offscreen items
- Asset optimizations: compress (Brotli/gzip), serve via CDN, set caching headers, use HTTP/2
- SSR/PRerender or hydrate critical UI to improve Time to First Paint
Backend diagnostics and fixes:
- Measure: use APM (e.g., New Relic), Node profiling tools (clinic, 0x), log slow queries
- Database: add proper indexes, paginate, optimize queries, use prepared statements
- Caching: introduce Redis for frequently-read data and rate-limited endpoints
- Concurrency: use clustering (node cluster or PM2), ensure connection pooling for DB
- Move heavy work off request loop to background workers/queues (Bull, RabbitMQ)
- Use streaming responses where appropriate and gzip responses
- Rate limiting and backpressure to protect services under spikes
- Monitor, set alerts, and iterate based on metrics
- Example code-level: memoize expensive child render, replace map+filter in render with precomputed arrays, enable gzip middleware (compression), use helmet and proper timeouts

flashcards.front: What are the core concepts of React (components, props, state, JSX, virtual DOM)?
flashcards.back: Components are the building blocks (functional or class) that return UI. Props are read-only inputs passed from parent to child. State is local, mutable data inside a component updated via setState (class) or useState (hooks). JSX is a syntax that compiles to React.createElement calls. The virtual DOM is an in-memory representation React diffs against the real DOM and applies minimal updates via reconciliation. Data flows unidirectionally (top-down).

flashcards.front: What are React Hooks, their rules, and common hooks to know?
flashcards.back: Hooks let functional components have state and lifecycle behavior. Common hooks: useState (state), useEffect (side effects and cleanup; dependency array controls when it runs), useRef (persistent mutable refs), useContext (consume Context), useReducer (complex state), useMemo/useCallback (memoization). Rules: call hooks only at the top level and only from React functions or custom hooks; custom hooks must start with "use". Manage effect dependencies carefully to avoid stale closures or infinite loops.

flashcards.front: How does reconciliation and list keying work, and what are common React performance optimizations?
flashcards.back: Reconciliation diffs virtual DOM trees to compute updates; stable, unique keys on list items let React match elements across renders. Avoid using array index as key when items can reorder. Optimizations: prevent unnecessary re-renders with React.memo (components), useMemo/useCallback (cache expensive computations or stable callbacks), split state to minimize affected subtrees, lazy-load routes/components with React.lazy + Suspense, use windowing/virtualization (react-window) for long lists, and profile with React DevTools to find bottlenecks. Also avoid heavy work in render and prefer async/debounced updates when appropriate.

company_brief.summary: GitLab is an enterprise DevSecOps platform and remote-first company that aims to “unlock every team to ship software at the speed of imagination.” It is used by millions (50+ million people) and more than 100,000 organizations, and emphasizes a handbook-first, transparent culture with benefits and remote work practices.
company_brief.what_they_do: GitLab provides a single platform for the entire software delivery lifecycle — from planning and source control to CI/CD, security, and deployment — with built-in security (SAST, SCA, Secret Detection, DAST, compliance) and flexible pricing (GitLab Flex). It offers the GitLab Duo Agent Platform for agentic software engineering (catalog of specialized agents, customizable agents and flows, event-driven execution, policy-driven governance, full traceability, and support for self‑hosted models) and GitLab Orbit as a context layer for AI agents. The platform is positioned for industries including financial services, public sector, telecommunications, automotive, and education.

questions.prompt: Design a concurrent worker pool in Go that processes tasks from a queue. Explain how you would implement task dispatch, handle context cancellation and timeouts, provide backpressure, and perform a graceful shutdown.
questions.answer_outline:
- Use a buffered channel as the task queue and spawn N worker goroutines that range over the channel
- Use context.Context passed to workers for cancellation and timeouts; workers select on ctx.Done() and task channel
- Use sync.WaitGroup to wait for workers to finish after closing the queue
- Provide backpressure via bounded channel capacity and/or rate limiter (token bucket) so producers block or return errors
- Surface errors via a dedicated error channel or aggregated result channel
- Use preStop hooks / SIGTERM handling to stop accepting new tasks, close the task channel, and wait for workers to drain

questions.prompt: How would you diagnose and fix a memory leak or high CPU usage in a Go service? List tools, signals to look for, and typical fixes.
questions.answer_outline:
- Tools: pprof (heap/cpu/goroutine/block profiles), runtime/trace, go tool pprof, race detector, net/http/pprof endpoint
- Signals: growth in heap/allocs over time, many stuck goroutines, high GC frequency or long GC pauses, CPU profile hotspots
- Steps: capture heap and CPU profiles, inspect allocation sites and flame graphs, list goroutines to find leaks or blocked routines
- Common fixes: reduce allocations (reuse buffers, sync.Pool), fix goroutine leaks (ensure contexts/channels closed), remove blocking syscalls, fix mutex contention, tune GC via GOGC if necessary
- Add monitoring/alerts for memory/cpu and regression tests with profiles

questions.prompt: You need to deploy a Go-based agent service for the GitLab Duo Agent Platform on Kubernetes. Describe the Kubernetes resources and configuration you would use to support scaling, rolling updates, health checks, configuration/secrets, and graceful shutdown.
questions.answer_outline:
- Use a Deployment for stateless agents (StatefulSet only if per-pod identity/storage needed); set resource requests/limits for scheduling
- Enable HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) based on CPU/memory or custom metrics; configure Cluster Autoscaler and node selectors/affinity if needed
- Configure liveness and readiness probes (HTTP/gRPC/probe endpoints) to control traffic during startup and upgrades
- Use rolling update strategy with appropriate maxUnavailable/maxSurge and PodDisruptionBudgets to balance availability
- Manage config via ConfigMaps and secrets via Kubernetes Secrets (mounted or env); use RBAC for least privilege
- Support graceful shutdown with preStop and SIGTERM handling in the Go app (drain work, stop accepting tasks, wait groups)
- Use namespaces, NetworkPolicies, and resource quotas for multi-tenant isolation; central logging/metrics (Prometheus/Grafana) for observability

questions.prompt: A Pod in your Kubernetes cluster running a Go service is repeatedly CrashLoopBackOff or being OOMKilled. Describe a troubleshooting checklist and the kubectl commands you'd run to find and resolve the root cause.
questions.answer_outline:
- kubectl describe pod <pod> to inspect events, restartReason, and status; kubectl get pods -o wide for node info
- kubectl logs <pod> (with --previous for crashed containers) to view runtime errors or stack traces
- Check containerStatus for OOMKilled or termination message and exit codes
- kubectl top pod/node to see resource usage; inspect resource requests/limits in Deployment/Pod spec
- If OOMKilled: increase memory request/limit, reduce memory usage in app (fix leaks, reduce batch sizes), or use vertical autoscaler
- If CrashLoopBackOff: examine liveness/readiness probes causing restarts, image pull or config errors, missing env/volume mounts
- Check node conditions and kubelet logs for node-level issues; use pprof in the app to capture heap if suspecting Go-level memory issues
- Consider reproducing locally with same resource limits to iterate quickly

flashcards.front: Explain goroutines and channels. How do they differ from OS threads, and when should you use channels vs sync primitives?
flashcards.back: Goroutines are lightweight user-space threads managed by the Go runtime scheduler (M:N scheduling) — thousands can run concurrently on a few OS threads. Channels are typed conduits for communication and synchronization between goroutines. Key points: use goroutines for concurrent tasks that are I/O-bound or easily decomposed; channels to pass data and synchronize without shared memory; use buffered channels for decoupling producers/consumers; select lets you wait on multiple channel ops; closing a channel signals no more values (don't close unless you are the sender); range on a channel reads until closed; deadlocks occur if all goroutines block. Use sync primitives (Mutex, Cond, WaitGroup, Atomic) when you need fine-grained control or to protect shared mutable state — channels are higher-level and encourage message-passing style.

flashcards.front: Describe Go's type system basics: interfaces, method receivers, pointer vs value behavior, and common pitfalls (nil interfaces, embedding).
flashcards.back: Interfaces are satisfied implicitly: a type implements an interface by implementing its methods. Method receivers can be value or pointer: value receivers get a copy (suitable for immutable or small types), pointer receivers can modify the receiver and avoid copying large structs. A pointer receiver means only *T implements the interface if methods are defined on *T; value receiver methods make both T and *T implement the interface. Nil interface pitfall: an interface value is a (type, value) pair — an interface holding a typed nil (e.g., (*T)(nil)) is not equal to nil. Embedding promotes fields/methods from embedded types (composition) and can be used to implement forwarding; beware method name collisions. Use type assertions (value, ok) or type switches to inspect concrete types.

flashcards.front: What are important memory and tooling considerations in Go: GC, escape analysis, slices vs arrays, and essential tools/commands?
flashcards.back: Go has a garbage collector optimized for low pause times; write memory-friendly code (avoid large allocations and long-lived roots). Escape analysis determines whether a variable is allocated on the stack or heap — prefer stack allocation by keeping values local and avoiding taking addresses that outlive scope. Slices are flexible, referencing an underlying array with length and capacity; slicing may keep the underlying array alive (leaking memory) if small subslices reference large arrays. Use make for slices, maps, channels; use new rarely (zeroed pointer). Essential tools: go mod (dependency/versioning), go build/run, go test (unit tests and benchmarks), go vet (static checks), go fmt (formatting), go tool pprof (profiling), and -race (race detector). For performance, profile CPU/heap and fix hotspots rather than micro-optimize.

flashcards.front: Explain the high-level Kubernetes architecture and the role of its main components.
flashcards.back: Kubernetes has a control plane and worker nodes. Control plane: API Server (central control, REST interface), etcd (cluster state store), Controller Manager (reconciles desired state), Scheduler (assigns pods to nodes). Node components: kubelet (manages pods/containers on the node), kube-proxy (service networking/routing), container runtime (e.g., containerd). Namespaces provide multi-tenancy/segmentation; labels/selectors enable grouping. For HA, run multiple control-plane instances with etcd clustered and use load-balancing for the API server.

flashcards.front: What are the core API objects for deploying apps and how do you choose between them?
flashcards.back: Core objects: Pod (single or co-located containers), ReplicaSet (ensures N pod replicas), Deployment (declarative rollout/rollbacks for stateless apps), StatefulSet (stable network IDs and storage for stateful apps), DaemonSet (one pod per node), Job/CronJob (batch tasks). Services expose pods: ClusterIP (in-cluster), NodePort, LoadBalancer; Ingress manages HTTP routing. ConfigMap/Secret inject config and sensitive data. PersistentVolume/PersistentVolumeClaim + StorageClass provide persistent storage. Use Deployment for stateless, StatefulSet for ordered startup/unique identities/persistent volumes, DaemonSet for node-level agents.

flashcards.front: Key operational commands and troubleshooting steps for common issues in Kubernetes.
flashcards.back: Useful kubectl: get/describe/logs/exec/port-forward/top -n <ns>. Check pod status/events (kubectl describe pod, kubectl get events) for CrashLoopBackOff or probe failures. Use kubectl logs -c <container>, kubectl exec to inspect container. For rollout issues: kubectl rollout status/undo. Inspect nodes (kubectl get nodes, describe node) for Ready, disk pressure, or Kubelet errors. Check resource limits and OOMKills, use kubectl top for metrics. Network problems: check CNI, kube-proxy, and DNS (coredns). Storage issues: verify PVC->PV binding and access modes. For RBAC issues: review Roles/ClusterRoles and RoleBindings. Collect events, describe resources, and reproduce with simplified manifests to isolate faults.
